**A Song to Her Ancient Lover**

Ancient love, for whom alone
All the flattering youth I've known
I defy—long may it be

Now by age's frost possessed,
From its icy hold released,
And soothed by my reviving hand,
In former warmth and strength shall stand.
All a lover's wish can reach,
My love, for thy joy, shall teach;
And for thy pleasure shall improve
All that art can add to love.
Yet still I love thee without art,
Ancient keeper of my heart.

---

outputs.L2:
**Elderly beloved, for whose sake**
For your affection I turn away all the charming young men who court me. May many years pass before you become elderly—suffering, trembling, feeble, and chilled. Instead, remain exactly as you are now, aged darling of my heart.

Upon your shriveled, parched lips—which resemble empty, unplanted trenches—I will lavish tender, thoughtful kisses that will bring back your youthful warmth. In the same way, gentle autumn rains sometimes descend and summon back a fleeting springtime. I will never leave your side, aged darling of my heart.

That finer part of you, which women would be too modest to mention aloud, now trapped in the chilly hold of old age, will be freed from that frost. Comforted and awakened by my restoring touch, it will rise once more with its old strength and heat.

Whatever a lover might possibly desire, my devotion will instruct for your delight, and for your enjoyment, my love will refine every skillful technique that enhances passion. Even so, I cherish you plainly and sincerely, without any pretense—aged darling of my heart.

# Devotion to an Aged Lover

The speaker declares her wholehearted commitment to an older man, casting aside the eager pursuits of flattering young suitors in favor of the one she truly cherishes. Though youthful admirers press their attentions upon her, she finds no appeal in their charms, for her heart belongs entirely to her aged beloved.

She expresses a tender wish that her "ancient person" might remain exactly as he is, untouched by further decline. With genuine affection, she hopes to hold back the encroaching frailties of old age, delaying their arrival for as long as time will allow, so that she may enjoy his company undiminished.

To this end, she promises to shower affectionate kisses upon his withered lips, seeking to rekindle the warmth of his youth. She likens her devotion to the gentle showers of autumn, which, falling upon the fading year, recall the freshness and vitality of spring—suggesting that her love can restore what age has begun to take away.

Beyond mere tenderness, she vows to revive his physical passion through her caring touch. With patient devotion, she promises to free his "nobler part" from the numbing grip of age, restoring the vigor that the years have diminished.

Finally, she pledges to devote herself to teaching and refining every form of love and pleasure for his delight, offering him joys both old and new. Yet through all of this, she assures him that her love remains sincere and free of pretense—an honest devotion given not from obligation or deception, but from the truth of her own heart.

# On Loving an Ancient Person

In this tender and quietly provocative poem, a young woman speaks directly to her aged lover, weaving together images of seasonal renewal and intimate devotion to make a promise both bold and gentle. She does not shrink from the difference in their years; instead, she embraces it, transforming what convention might deem an unlikely pairing into an occasion for celebrating love's power to warm and restore.

The speaker opens by addressing her beloved with an affectionate familiarity, calling him her "ancient person" not as an insult but as a term of endearment. Where others might see only frailty and the encroachment of winter upon his life, she sees a landscape ripe for tender cultivation. Drawing upon the natural cycle of the seasons, she likens her love to the returning spring—a force capable of thawing what has grown cold and coaxing new vigor from ground that others have written off as barren. Her imagery insists that age need not mean the end of passion or warmth; rather, it can become the very soil in which devotion takes its deepest root.

As the poem unfolds, the young woman makes her intentions explicit through language of physical closeness and care. She pledges the reviving warmth of her own body, promising to press her youthful heat against his chilled limbs and to breathe life back into him through her touch. This is not a fleeting or superficial attraction but an active, generous devotion. She casts herself as a nurse to his cold, a fire against his frost, offering the gift of her vitality freely and without condition. Every caress carries the promise of renewal, as though her love alone might reverse the slow retreat of his youthful heat and vigor.

Yet the heart of the poem lies not merely in these sensuous promises but in the sincerity that underlies them. The speaker takes pains to affirm that her affection is genuine and unpretentious—free from calculation, mockery, or the pursuit of some hidden gain. She loves her ancient person simply and truly, and she is unashamed to declare it. In doing so, she quietly resists the assumptions of a world that would confine desire to the young and the conventionally beautiful. Her devotion becomes a form of gentle defiance, challenging the expectation that love and companionship must always follow the well-worn paths of age-matched romance.

Ultimately, the poem celebrates a love that transcends the boundaries of time and physical decline. By binding together the imagery of seasonal rebirth with the intimacy of physical tenderness, the young woman transforms her elderly lover from an object of pity into a worthy recipient of passionate, enduring affection. Her closing affirmation—that hers is a sincere and constant love—stands as both a personal vow and a broader statement about the nature of devotion itself: that true love answers not to the calendar but to the heart, and that warmth freely given can defy even the cold advance of the years.

When we study **ancient** cultures, from the pyramid builders of Egypt to the philosophers of Greece, we discover that human questions have remained remarkably consistent. These questions have accompanied us **all** along our journey as a species, and the answers proposed by **ancient** thinkers still resonate today.

Consider how **long** these teachings have survived:

- Philosophical texts written thousands of years ago remain in print
- Traditional practices continue to influence **all** aspects of contemporary life

The fact that this knowledge has lasted so **long** speaks to its universal value. What worked for our ancestors often works for us **all**, because human nature itself changes very slowly.

## Carrying Forward the Torch

We are **all** inheritors of this vast treasury of understanding. As we move forward through time, it becomes our responsibility to preserve these **ancient** insights and pass them along to future generations.

The journey has been **long**, but the wisdom endures—reminding us that some truths truly last forever.
